passages.original: Prædicamentorum vero in hoc ratio constituta est,in quo hæ duæ partes interpretationis res intellectibus subjectas desi- gnent.Nam quoniam decem ras omnino in umni natura reperiuntur, decem quoque intellectus erunt, quos intellectus, quoniam nomina et verba significant,decem omnino erunt prædicamenta,quæ verbis atquo nominibus designentur;duo vero quædam sunt, id est nomen et verbum quas ipsos significent intellectus.Sunt igitur elementa interpretationis verba et nomina,proprie vero partes quibus ipsa constat interpretatio suut orationes.Orationum vero alia? sunt perfectæ,aliæ imperfectæ. Perfectae sunt ex quibus plene id quod dicitur valet intelligi;i mperfectae vero in quibus aliquid adhuc plenius animus exspectat audire, ut est Socrates cum Platone.N ullo enimad- dito,orationis intellectus adhuc pendet ac titubat,et auditor aliquid ultra exspectat audire.Perfectarum vero orationum partes quinque sunt. Deprecativa, ut:Jupiter omnipotens,precibussi ecers uWs,Ua deinde auxilium, pater,atque hæc omina firma.lm- perativa, ut : Vade age, nate, voca zephyros et la- bere pennis, Interrogativa, ut : Dis mihi,Damæta, cujum pecus, an Melibœi ?
passages.english: The account of the categories, however, is grounded in this: that these two parts of interpretation signify the things that underlie the concepts. For since ten things in all are found in the whole of nature, there will also be ten concepts; and since names and verbs signify these concepts, there will be ten categories in all, which are designated by verbs and names; but there are two particular things, namely the name and the verb, which signify these concepts themselves. The elements of interpretation, then, are verbs and names, but the parts, properly speaking, of which interpretation itself consists are sentences. Of sentences, some are complete, others incomplete. Complete ones are those from which what is said can be fully understood; incomplete ones are those in which the mind still expects to hear something more fully, as in "Socrates with Plato." For if nothing is added, the understanding of the sentence still hangs and wavers, and the hearer expects to hear something further. Of complete sentences there are five kinds. The precative, as: "Almighty Jupiter, if you are moved by any prayers, then give [us] aid, father, and confirm these omens." The imperative, as: "Go then, son, call the Zephyrs and glide on your wings." The interrogative, as: "Tell me, Damoetas, whose flock [is this]? Is it Meliboeus'?"
passages.notes: The verse quotations (Virgil, Aeneid 2 and 4, Eclogue 3) are badly garbled by the scan ('precibussi ecers uWs,Ua deinde'); translated as 'precibus si flecteris ullis, da deinde auxilium'. 'ras' read as 'res', 'umni' as 'omni', 'Dis' as 'Dic'.

passages.original: Non esse namque proprium Aristotelio hinc conatur ostendere,quoniam quasdam AribLoteles in principio libri hujus deintellectibus animi tractat,quos intellectus animæ passiones vocavit,et de his se plenius in libris de anima disputasse commemorat.Et quo. niam passiones animae vccabat, vel tristitiam, vel gaudium, vel cupiditatem,ve] alias hujusmodi afTe- ctiones dicit Andronicus ex hoc probari hunc librum Aristotelis non esse, quod de hujusmodi affectionibus nihil in lihri de anima tractavisset,non inteIH- gens in hoc libro Aristotelem passioned animae non pro affectionibus, sed pro intellectibus posuisse.Нis Alexander multa alia addit argumenta cur hoc opus maxime Aristotelis esse videatur.Ea namque dicuntur hic quae sententiis Aristotelis quae sunt de enuntiativa oratione consentiant;illud quoque, quod stylus ipse propter brevitatem pressior ab Aristotelis obscu- ritatc non discrepat;
passages.english: For he tries to show that it is not Aristotle's own on these grounds: that at the beginning of this book Aristotle treats of certain concepts of the mind, which he called affections of the soul, and mentions that he has discussed these more fully in the books On the Soul. And since he called them affections of the soul, Andronicus says they are sadness, or joy, or desire, or other affections of this kind, and that it is proved from this that this book is not Aristotle's, because he had treated nothing about such affections in the books On the Soul; he does not understand that in this book Aristotle used 'affections of the soul' not for emotions but for concepts. To these [objections] Alexander adds many other arguments why this work seems most surely to be Aristotle's. For things are said here which agree with Aristotle's views on the declarative sentence; and also that the style itself, compressed on account of its brevity, does not differ from Aristotle's obscurity;

Sed de hoc quoqne aperte quidom videlur usteRdere. ait enim an certe neque hæc sunt imaginationes, sed non sine imaginationibus sunt. Id enim quod hic sermo significat,qui est Socrates, vel alius, simplex ponesL quidem imaginatio. sed inLellectus,qui intellectus præter imaginationem fieri non potest.Sensus enim atque imaginatio qUiP- dam primæfiguræ sunt,supraquas velut fundameuto quodam superveniens intelligentia nititur.Nam sicut pictores solent designare lineatim corpus atque sulh sternere in corpore ubi coloribus cujuslibet expri- mant vultum,sic sensus atque imaginatio naturaliter in anima perceptione substernitur.
passages.english: "Surely these are not images either, but they do not exist without images." This statement shows that images are one thing and concepts another, and that affirmations and negations come about from the combination of concepts; for which reason he also raised the doubt whether the first concepts were certain images. We call 'first concepts' those which grasp a simple thing, as if someone should say 'Socrates' alone; and he doubts whether a concept of this kind, which contains in itself nothing either true or false, is a concept or an image of Socrates himself. But on this too he seems to show [his view] plainly, for he says: "Or surely these are not images, but they are not without images." For what this word signifies, namely 'Socrates' or anything else, is not a simple image but a concept, a concept which cannot come about apart from an image. For sense and imagination are certain first shapes, on which understanding, coming upon them as on a kind of foundation, rests. For just as painters are accustomed to sketch a body in outline and lay down [a base] on the body, where they may express with colours the face of anyone, so sense and imagination are naturally laid down beneath perception in the soul.
passages.notes: 'simplex ponesL quidem imaginatio' is corrupt; read as 'non est simplex quidem imaginatio'. 'sulh sternere' read as 'substernere'. The quotation is from Aristotle, De anima 3.8.

passages.original: Nomina vero et verba non curta quaedam, sed perfecta significant:quare recta Aristotelissen' tentia est, quaecunque in verbis nominibusque versantur, ea neque sensus, neque imaginationis, sed solam significare intellectuum qualitatem .Undeillud quoque ab Aristotele fluentes Peripateci rectissime posuere,tres esse orationes,unam quæ scribi possit litteris, alteram quæ voce proferri, tertiam quæ cogitatione connectitur, unamque intellectibus ,alteram voce,terliam litteris cc.ntineri.Quocirca quoniam id quod significaretur a vocibus intellectus esse Aristoteles putabat, nomina vero et verba significativa esse in eorum erat diffinitionibus positurus, recte quorum essent significativa prædixit, erroremque lectoris ex multiplici veterum lite venientem sententiæ suæ manifestatione compescuit,atque hoc modo nihil in eo deprehenditur essesuperfluum,nihilque ab ordinis continuatione sejunctum. Quaerit vero Porphyrius cur ita dixerit : Sunt ergo ea quae sunt in voce, et non sic, sunt ergo voces; et rursus cur ita et ea quae scribuntur, et non dixerit, et litteræ, quod resolvit hoc modo. Dictum est tres esse apud Peripateticos orationes, unam quæ litteris scribitur, aliam quae profertur in voce, terti am quæconjunge- retur in auimo.
passages.english: Names and verbs, however, signify not certain incomplete things but complete ones. Therefore Aristotle's view is correct, that whatever is contained in verbs and names signifies the quality neither of sense nor of imagination, but only of understandings. Hence the Peripatetics, flowing from Aristotle, quite rightly laid down that there are three kinds of speech: one that can be written in letters, another that can be uttered by the voice, a third that is joined together in thought; and that one is contained in understandings, another in the voice, the third in letters. Therefore, since Aristotle thought that what is signified by spoken sounds is understandings, and he was going to state in their definitions that names and verbs are significative, he rightly said beforehand of what things they are significative, and by making his view plain he checked the reader's error arising from the manifold dispute of the ancients; and in this way nothing in it is found superfluous, and nothing detached from the continuity of the order. Porphyry, however, asks why he said, 'Those, then, that are in the voice', and not thus, 'They are, then, spoken sounds'; and again why he said 'and those that are written', and not 'and letters'. He resolves it in this way. It has been said that among the Peripatetics there are three kinds of speech: one that is written in letters, another that is uttered in the voice, a third that is joined together in the mind.

passages.english: But to show that understandings and things exist by nature, he says that among all people the understandings are the same, of which the spoken sounds are significative, and again that among all the things are the same, of which the affections of the soul are likenesses; as it is: 'but the things of which these, namely those in the voice, are primarily signs, the affections of the soul, are the same for all, and the things of which these are likenesses are also the same.' He spoke of 'affections of the soul' because it has been carefully shown elsewhere that every utterance of an animal is produced either from an affection of the soul or on account of an affection. passages.english: or if I say "Socrates walks," this is the same as if I said "Socrates is walking." Therefore, whenever there is a composition of this kind, which by the verb 'to be' either establishes a substance or conjoins things, it is called an affirmation, and in it the nature of true and false is observed. And since every negation is set against a predication—for the negation of this affirmation, "Socrates is," is not the one which says "Not Socrates is," but the one which declares "Socrates is not"—the 'not' of negation is applied to that which Socrates was said to be, so that we say that not to be which was said before to be. Therefore, since the negation added to what in the affirmation was either established or conjoined according to being separates either the very establishment of the substance or else the conjunction made through what was said, [namely] that something is, it is called division.
passages.notes: Syntax of the long sentence is loose; 'estjel' read as 'est, ei'.

passages.original: Catonis autem vel Catoni,et quæcunque talia sunt non sunt nomina sed casus nominis. Ratio au-tem ejus est in aliis quidem eadem, sed diflert. Quoniam c"m eat, vel (uit, vel erit, adjunctum, neque verum, neque falsum eat, nomen vero semper, ut Catonis est, vel non est, nondum enim aliquid dicit verum aut falsum.
passages.english: 'Of Cato' or 'to Cato', and whatever are of that kind, are not names but cases of a name. Their definition is the same in other respects, but it differs in this: that with 'is', 'was' or 'will be' added it is neither true nor false, whereas a name always is; for example, 'Of Cato is' or 'is not': this does not yet say anything true or false.
passages.notes: This is the Aristotelian lemma (De int. 2). Read 'cum est' for 'c"m eat'; 'est' for 'eat'. The clause 'nomen vero semper' appears to compress Aristotle's point that a name with 'is' is always true or false.

Horum enim discrepantia est a nomine,quod nomen rectum junctum cum est, vel non est, enuntiationem facit, ut si quis dicat, Socrates est, hoc verum vel falsum est. Si enim vivente Socrate diceretur, verum es- set., svero mortuo, asum esse, quare affirmatio, est.Si quis autem dicat,Socrates non est, rursus fa- . cit negationem,et in ea quoque veritas vel falsitas invenitur.Ergo omne nomen rectum junctum cum est vel non est, enuntiationem coniicit.
passages.english: but here he gave a word to this expression, saying, "but let it be an indefinite name": not simply a name, since it signifies with no limitation, but an indefinite name, since it signifies many things, and those indefinitely. But this does not happen only to expressions of this kind, that they cannot simply be placed under 'name'; there are certain others which have all the accidents of a name and signify definitely, but by some other difference cannot simply be called names, such as the oblique cases, as when we say 'of Cato', 'to Cato', 'Cato' (accusative), and the rest. Their difference from a name is this: a name in the nominative, joined with 'is' or 'is not', makes a statement, as if someone says "Socrates is", this is true or false. For if it were said while Socrates was alive, it would be true, but if after his death, false; so it is an affirmation. And if someone says "Socrates is not", he in turn makes a negation, and in it too truth or falsity is found. Therefore every nominative name joined with 'is' or 'is not' produces a statement.

passages.original: Hi vero obliqui casus juncti cum est, vel cum non est, enuntiationem nulla ratione perficiunt. Enuntiatio namque est perfectus orationis intellectus in quem veritas aut falsitas cadit.Si quis ergo dicat,Catonis est,nondum est plena sententia ; quid enim sit Catonis non dicitur, atque eodem modo, Catoni est, vel Catonem est. In his ergo quoniam cum est vel non est injuncta,enuntiationem non perficiunt, est quaedam a nomine discrepantia,quanquam sint no.
passages.english: These oblique cases, when joined with 'is' or with 'is not', in no way complete a statement. For a statement is a complete understanding of speech into which truth or falsity falls. So if someone says 'Of Cato is', it is not yet a full sentence; for what is of Cato is not said; and in the same way 'To Cato is' or 'Cato [accusative] is'. In these, then, since when 'is' or 'is not' is joined to them they do not complete a statement, there is a certain difference from the name, although they are
