passages.original: Verbum autem cum principaliter actus passionesque significet, cum ipHis actibus et passionibus temporis quoque vim trahit, ut in eo quod dico lego,actionem quidem quamdam principaliter monstrat.Hoc verbum,sed cum ea ipsa agendi significatione præsens quoque tempus adducit,atque ideo non ait verbum significare tempus,sed consignificare.Nequeenim principaliterverbum significat tempus (boc enim nominis est), sed cum aliis quae principaliter significat,vim quoquetemporis inducit et inserit.Ergo cum nomen et verbum voces significativae sint, et secundum placitum, additum verbo quod consignificat tempus,a nomine segregatur,ut enim sæpe dictum est, nomen significare tempus poterit, verbum vero consignificare, et sicut in diffinitione nominis addidit.nihi! omnino partes separa- ratas a tota compositione nominis designare,propter orationes quae nominibus essent compositæ, ut est Plato et Socrates, ita quoque in verbo addidit, nihil extra verbi partes significare,propler eas orationes quas verba componunt,ut est ambulare et currere, haec enim oratio ex verbis est composita, et singula verba et in ipsa oratione et praeter eam per se ipsa significant.
passages.english: A verb, though it principally signifies actions and passions, draws along with those actions and passions the force of time as well; as in saying 'I read', this verb principally shows a certain action, but along with that very signification of acting it brings in present time too; and therefore he does not say that a verb signifies time, but that it co-signifies. For a verb does not principally signify time (that belongs to a name), but together with the other things which it principally signifies, it brings in and inserts the force of time as well. Therefore, since name and verb are significative spoken sounds and by convention, the verb is separated from the name by the addition that it co-signifies time; for, as has often been said, a name can signify time, while a verb co-signifies it. And just as in the definition of the name he added that its parts, separated from the whole composition of the name, designate nothing at all, on account of phrases composed of names, such as 'Plato and Socrates', so also in the case of the verb he added that its parts signify nothing separately, on account of those phrases which verbs compose, such as 'to walk and to run'; for this phrase is composed of verbs, and the single verbs signify by themselves both within the phrase itself and outside it.

passages.original: Est hic quæstio,non enim verum videri potest,quod ait; constituit enim quod dicit illlellectum,et quod audit quiescit.Nam neque qui dicit constituitintet' Jectum,neque quod audit quiescit; deest enim quiddam sermoni vel nomini, ut si quis dicat Socrates, mox audientis animus requirit quidSocrates,facitne aliquid an patitur? et nondum audientis intellectus estquietus,cum horum aliquid requirit,et in verbo idem est,cum dico legit,quis legat animusaudientis requirit.
passages.english: There is a question here, for what he says cannot seem true: [namely] that the one who speaks establishes understanding and the one who hears comes to rest. For neither does the speaker establish understanding nor does the hearer come to rest; for something is lacking to the word or name, as when someone says "Socrates", the mind of the hearer at once asks what about Socrates—is he doing something or undergoing something?—and the hearer's understanding is not yet at rest when it asks for one of these; and the same holds in the verb: when I say "reads", the hearer's mind asks who is reading.

passages.original: nam si affirmatio et negatio in inteUec- . tuum compositionibus invenitur,ut supra,jam docuit neque sola nomina dictanequeverba aut affirmationem, aut ullam facient. negationem. Pluribus enim modis docuit Aristoteles alias non in rebus, sed in intellectibus veritatem falsitatemque esse constitutam, quoniam si in rebus veritas falsitasve esset, una res sola aut affirmatio esset, aut quæ ei contraria est, negatio.
passages.english: for if affirmation and negation are found in compositions of understandings, as he has already taught above, neither names nor verbs said on their own will make either an affirmation or any negation. For Aristotle taught in several ways elsewhere that truth and falsity are established not in things but in understandings, since if truth or falsity were in things, a single thing alone would be either an affirmation or, what is contrary to it, a negation.

passages.original: Sed hoc Aristoteles negat, et Alexander multisin eo nititurargumentis,monstrans orationem non esse instrumentum naturale.Aristo- te]es vero ita utitur dicens: Estautem oratio omnis quidem significativa, non sicut instrumentum,tanquam si diceret: Est quidem omnis oratio significativa,non tamen naturaliter, instrumentum enim boc demonstrat, tanquam si diceret naturaliter signif]- care. Quod qui instrumentumorationemesse negant, non eam naturaliter significare dicunt,sed ad placi- tum.Naturalium enim rerum naturalia sunt instrumenta. Idcirco autem instrumentum pro natura posuit, quod (ut dictum est) Plato omnium artium instrumenta, secundum naturam ipsarum artiumcon- sistere proponebat. Et Alexander quidem non esse instrumentum orationem sic ingrediturapprobare. Omnis, inquit, naturalium actuum supellex, ipsa quoque naturalis est, ut in sensu quoniam natura rJatur,pjus quoque supellex est naturalis,ut oculus.
passages.english: But Aristotle denies this, and Alexander strives on this point with many arguments, showing that speech is not a natural instrument. Aristotle puts it thus, saying: 'Every speech is significative, not as an instrument', as if he were saying: every speech is indeed significative, yet not by nature; for 'instrument' indicates this, as if he were saying 'signifies by nature'. For those who deny that speech is an instrument say that it signifies not by nature but by convention. For natural things have natural instruments. He put 'instrument' for 'nature' because, as has been said, Plato proposed that the instruments of all the arts are established according to the nature of those arts. And Alexander undertakes to prove that speech is not an instrument as follows. All the equipment of natural acts, he says, is itself natural too; as in sense, since it is given by nature, its equipment too is natural, such as the eye.
passages.notes: 'rJatur,pjus' read as 'datur, ejus'.

passages.original: Erf(o necesse est omnem enuntiativam orationem si simplex sit, verbum in praedicatione retinere,ut in eadem ipsa,cum dico, sol oritur, oritur verbum est, vel quod idem valeat, ut. est, Socrates non ambulat , non ambulat enim infinitum verbum est, et verbum quidem non est, sed eamdem vim retinet quam verbum. Casus etiam verbi ponitur sæpe, ut Socrates fuit; subjectus vero terminus non semper consistit in nomine, potest enim infinitum nomen habere,ut cum dico,non homo ambulat, potest et verbum, ut cum dico, ambulare. moveri est;ergo fut arbitror)plene monstra- tum est non semper subjectum nomen esse, sed semper prædicatumin solo vero consistere.
passages.english: Therefore every declarative sentence, if it is simple, must have a verb in the predicate, as in the same [example], when I say "the sun rises", 'rises' is a verb; or something of equivalent force, as "Socrates does not walk", for 'does not walk' is an indefinite verb, and it is not indeed a verb, but it has the same force as a verb. A case of the verb is also often used, as "Socrates was". The subject term, however, does not always consist in a name, for it can have an indefinite name, as when I say "Not-man walks", and it can have a verb, as when I say "To walk is to be moved." Therefore, as I think, it has been fully shown that the subject is not always a name, but that the predicate always consists in a verb alone.
passages.notes: 'in solo vero' read as 'in solo verbo'.

passages.original: Et quemadmodum in his quae hypotheticae vel conditionales dicuntur,conjunctiones vim propositionis te- nent,sic in simplicibus propositionibus prædicatio vim obtinet,unde et Graece quoque tales propositiones ϰϰτηγοριϰαί,id est prædicativæ,dicuntur,scilicet quæsun tsimplices,quod inbijtotampropositionem obtineat prædicatio, atque ideo Aristoteles ait, ex verbo vel casu fieri simplicem enuntiationem.Nam praeter id quod continet totam propositionem prædicativam, scilicet praeter prædicationem, enuntiatio non fit,unde est ut negatio quoque non ad subjeclum, sed ad praedicatum semper apteturNam, cum dico, sol oritur,non est hujus negatio,non sol oritur,sed illa quae est,sol non oritur, atque ideo negatio ad subjectum posita,non facit contrariam propositionem, ad praedicatum vero reddit contrariam.
passages.english: And just as in those [propositions] called hypothetical or conditional the conjunctions hold the force of the proposition, so in simple propositions the predication holds the force; hence in Greek too such propositions are called *katēgorikai*, that is, predicative, namely those that are simple, because in them the predication holds the whole proposition; and therefore Aristotle says that a simple statement comes from a verb or a case [of a verb]. For apart from what contains the whole predicative proposition, namely apart from the predication, no statement comes about; hence the negation too is always fitted not to the subject but to the predicate. For when I say 'The sun rises', its negation is not 'Not the sun rises' but 'The sun does not rise'; and therefore a negation placed at the subject does not make a contrary proposition, but placed at the predicate it renders [one] contrary.
passages.notes: Greek garbled ('ϰϰτηγοριϰαί' for κατηγορικαί). 'contrary' here evidently means 'opposed/contradictory'.

passages.original: Siveautem his propositionibus omnis addatur,ut est, omnis homo vivit, sive nullus, ut nullus apis vivit, sive aliquis,ut aliquis homo vivit,vel aliquis homo non vivit, quoniam termini ipsi duo sunt, simplex vocatur propositio,composita vero si ultra terminos duo8 enuntiat,ut est Plato philosophusin lycaeo ambulat.Hic enim quatuor sunt termini, vel si tres sint, ut Plato philosophus ambulat,hæ quoquesi eis omnis, aut nuDus, aut aliquis addatur, eodem modo compositae sunt.Ergo una vel multiplex oratio intelligitur,si unum vel multa significat, et de propria significatione semper judicatur.
passages.english: Whether 'every' is added to these propositions, as 'Every man lives', or 'no', as 'No bee lives', or 'some', as 'Some man lives' or 'Some man does not live', since the terms themselves are two, the proposition is called simple; but composite if it states more than two terms, as 'Plato the philosopher walks in the Lyceum'. For here there are four terms; or if there are three, as 'Plato the philosopher walks', these too, if 'every', 'no' or 'some' is added to them, are composite in the same way. Therefore a speech is understood as one or multiple according as it signifies one thing or many, and it is always judged by its own signification.

passages.original: Potest quidem fieri ut composita sit, una tamen oratio sit significatione composita dictione,ut est animal rationale,mortale, mentisetdisciplinæ capax: haec quidemplurasunt, sed his una substantia subjecta est,id est homo. Quare una quoque sententiaest.Sin vero quia dicat, Socrates et ambulat, et loquitur, et cogitat, multa sunt.Diversa sunt Anim, et quod ambulat, et quod loquitur,et quod eogital.Quare erit aliquando com- posita quidem oratio,una tamen:sed quoniam com- , posita oratio aliquoties quidem continue sine conjunctione dicitur,aliquoties conjunctione copulatur, fiunt binc quatuor differenliæ.
passages.english: It can indeed happen that a sentence is composite and yet is one in signification, composite in expression, as "animal, rational, mortal, capable of mind and learning": these are indeed several things, but one substance underlies them, namely man. Hence the meaning too is one. But if someone says "Socrates both walks and talks and thinks," these are many. For walking, talking and thinking are different. So a sentence will sometimes be composite yet one. But since a composite sentence is sometimes spoken continuously without a conjunction, and sometimes linked by a conjunction, four distinctions arise from this.

passages.original: Sive autem incompositae, et sive compositæ,et uno quidem modo una oratio dicitur cum sine conjunctione'non est.A]iovero cum una.n rem significat, rursus uno dictur modo multiplex oratio cum aliqua conjunctione non copulatur, alio vero cum plura significat, atque hoc est, quod ait : Est autem una oratio enuntiativa quæ unum significat vel conjunctione una.Plures autem quæ plura et non unum,vel inconjunctæ;est enim (ut dictum esl) du- pliciter una oratio,vel quando cum conjunctioneest, vel cu m unam rem significat.Multiplex autem oratio e?t,vel quae multa significat, vel quæ sine conjun- cttone conjungitur, multas enim orationes vocavit eas quae sint multiplices,et vel significationis pluralitatem teneant, vel praeter conjunctiones sint. Quod autem ait,vpl inconjunctae, totum complexus est, multiplex est enim propositio vel si fuerit in- composita,quemadmodum est,Cato philosophus est. Multiplex etiam vel si fuerit composita ex terminis præter conjunctionem,quemadmodum dictum est, utPlatoAtheniensis in lycæo disputat:vel si compn- sUa sit ex propositionibus praeter conjunctionem, quemadmodum est,bomo est,animal est;vel si composita sit ex terminis conjunctione copulatis, utJ u- piter et Apollo dii sunt;
passages.english: Whether, then, [sentences are] uncompounded or compounded, in one way a sentence is called one when it is not without a conjunction, in another when it signifies one thing; again, in one way a sentence is called multiple when it is not joined by any conjunction, in another when it signifies many things. And this is what he says: 'A statement-making sentence is one if it signifies one thing or is one by conjunction. Those are many which signify many things and not one, or are unconjoined.' For (as has been said) a sentence is one in two ways, either when it is with a conjunction or when it signifies one thing. A sentence is multiple either when it signifies many things or when it is joined without a conjunction; for he called 'many sentences' those which are multiple, and which either hold a plurality of signification or are without conjunctions. And by saying 'or unconjoined' he has embraced the whole: for a proposition is multiple if it is uncompounded, as is 'Cato is a philosopher'. It is multiple also if it is compounded of terms without a conjunction, as was said, like 'Plato the Athenian discourses in the Lyceum'; or if it is compounded of propositions without a conjunction, as is 'a man is, an animal is'; or if it is compounded of terms joined by a conjunction, as 'Jupiter and Apollo are gods';
passages.notes: The opening clause 'cum sine conjunctione non est' is read as 'when it is not without a conjunction'. The example 'Cato is a philosopher' as multiple while uncompounded is odd (presumably via the many meanings of 'Cato'); the text may be corrupt.

passages.original: Quod vero ait, Harum autem,enuntiativarum sciliceloration um,dixit quarum hæc quidem simplex est enuntiatio, et quæ simplex est enuntiatio, ipse proposuit dicens, ut aliquid de aliquo subaudiendum est prædicemus, ul sihicsen- sus.Harum autem enuntiativarum orationum est simplex enuntiatio, si aJiquid unum de uno aliquo prædicemus, ut si dicam Plato disputat, de aliquo Platone aliquid, id est disputat, prædicavi. Et haee simplex est enuntiatio.Ideirco quoniam duobus terminis partibusque conjungitur. Si qua vero plures habeat terminos,etejus partes duorum terminorum muItitudinem egrediantur,illæ compositæ orationes dicuntur,et est enuntiatio composita hujusmodi: si dies est,lux est, dies enim est, et lux est.
passages.english: As for his saying 'Of these', namely of statement-making sentences, he said that one of them is a simple statement; and what a simple statement is he himself set out, saying 'as when we predicate something of something' — this must be understood — so that this is the sense: of these statement-making sentences, the simple statement is when we predicate some one thing of some one thing, as if I say 'Plato discourses', I have predicated something, namely 'discourses', of someone, Plato. And this is a simple statement, because it is joined from two terms and parts. But if any has more terms, and its parts go beyond the number of two terms, those are called composite sentences, and a composite statement is of this kind: 'if it is day, there is light'; for 'it is day' and 'there is light'.

passages.original: Multiplex autem vel cuj LIS partes conjunctione copulantur, quae multa significat, vel quae eonjun- ctione nonjungitur.Harum quoque simplex est,quæ duobus terminis constat,ut aliquid de aliquo, vel aliquid ab aliquo; alia vero composita,quæ ex simpli- cibus affirmationibus jungitur.Quod autem dicitali-I quid de aliquo, vel aliquid ab aliquo, tale est: Aliquid enim de aliquo affirmationem significat,utcum dico, Socrates dispulat,de aliquo Socrate aliquid,id est disputat, prædicavi, et lit affirmatio. Si autem dico,Socrates non disputat,a Socrate disputationem sejunxi,et ab eo abstuli,et hoc est negatio.Affirmatio enim de alia re aliam rem prædicat eique conjungit.Negatio vero a qualibet requamlibetremprædi- cando tollit,ergo hoc quod ait, aliquid dequo,affir.
passages.english: Multiple, moreover, is either [the sentence] whose parts are linked by a conjunction and which signifies many things, or that which is not joined by a conjunction. Of these, too, one kind is simple, which consists of two terms, as something of something, or something from something; the other is composite, which is joined from simple affirmations. What he says, 'something of something' or 'something from something', is this: 'something of something' signifies affirmation, as when I say "Socrates argues", I have predicated something, namely 'argues', of something, Socrates, and it is an affirmation. But if I say "Socrates does not argue", I have separated arguing from Socrates and taken it away from him, and this is negation. For affirmation predicates one thing of another and joins it to it; negation removes any thing from any thing by predicating. So by saying 'something of something' he signified a simple affirmation,
passages.notes: The opening clause is garbled ('cuj LIS'); read as 'cujus'; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Aspasius etiam consentit Alexandro: dicit enim Alexander eodem modo hie diffinisseArislotelem enuntilltionem,slcut alibi quoque, id est, in resolutoriis: illic enim ita propositionem, qua? est enuntiatio,diffinitione con- elusit dicens:Propositio ergo est oratio affirmativa vel negativa alicujus de aliquo,vel alicujus ab ali- I quo.Idem quoqueAspasius sequitur.Porphyrius autem sic dicit:Admirabilem esse subtilitatem diffinitionis, ex sua enim vi affirmationis et lJegationis, enuntiatio diffinita est.Ex terminis vero,ipsa afHr- matio,atque negatio,affirmatio namque in duobus terminis constans, aliquid alicui inesse significat.
passages.english: Aspasius also agrees with Alexander. For Alexander says that Aristotle defined the statement here in the same way as elsewhere too, that is, in the Analytics; for there he encompassed the proposition, which is a statement, in a definition, saying: 'A proposition, then, is a sentence affirming or denying something of something, or something from something.' Aspasius also follows the same. Porphyry, however, says this: that the subtlety of the definition is admirable, for the statement is defined from the proper force of affirmation and negation, while affirmation and negation themselves [are defined] from the terms; for affirmation, consisting in two terms, signifies that something belongs to something.

passages.original: dicit dies secundum terminos adesse monstravit,esl enim dieiest,aliquid alicui applicuit, sed tota hujusmodi propositionis vis est alquesse declarare: rursus cum dico, dies non est, aliquid alicui non esse pronuntio, sed tota vis hujus est non esse dicere;quare manifestum estse- cundumPorphyriumextotavi affirmationis et negationis enuntiationem esse descriptam, ex suis vero terminis ipsam affirmationem et negationem. Ait enim,affirmatio vero est enuntiatio alicuj us de ali quo in affirmationis diffinitione genus sumens;enuntiatio enim(ut dictum est)genusest affirmationis et negationis,quod ipse Aristoteles clarius demonstrat,qui in utrorumque diffinitione enuntiationis nomen ascripsit dicens: Affirmatio vero est enuntiatio.Hoc enim retulit ad genus,quod vero addidit alicujus de aliquo reduxit ad terminos, in simplici enim affil" matione aliquid de aliquo enuntiando prædicatur, ut ineo quod est, dies est,esse diem.
passages.english: [In this affirmation which] says 'it is day', he showed according to the terms that day is present; for 'it is day' applied something to something, but the whole force of such a proposition is to declare [that something] is. Again, when I say 'it is not day', I declare that something is not [present] to something, but the whole force of this is to say 'is not'. Hence it is clear that according to Porphyry the statement has been described from the whole force of affirmation and negation, but affirmation and negation themselves from their terms. For he says, 'An affirmation is a statement of something about something', taking the genus in the definition of affirmation; for statement (as has been said) is the genus of affirmation and negation, which Aristotle himself shows more clearly, who wrote the name 'statement' into the definition of both, saying 'An affirmation is a statement'. This he referred to the genus; but what he added, 'of something about something', he brought back to the terms; for in a simple affirmation something is predicated of something by stating it, as in 'it is day', being [is predicated] of day.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence; 'alquesse' read as 'aliquid esse'.

passages.original: Sed quoniam hoc tem- pus præsens designat, non solum de præsenti, inquit,loquimur,sed etiam de his temporibus quæ di- viduntur, ut hoc essa, et non esse, et in futurum veniat et in præteritum,ut aliquoties sic esse et non esse significet, id est sic ponat atque sic auferat, enuntiatio,utet praesens tempus ponat,etauferat,ut est,Socrates est,Socrates non est,et præteritum po- nat, et auferat, .ut Socrates fuit, Socrates non fuit, eodem ,quoque modo futurum, Socrates erit, Socra- tes non erit.Ergo in his omnibus temporibus secun- dum esse aliquid vel non esse aliquid ,id est secundum ponere, et auferre tota enuntiationis vis est;
passages.english: But since this designates present time, we speak, he says, not only of the present but also of those times which are divided, so that this 'to be' and 'not to be' may extend both to the future and to the past, so that the statement sometimes signifies 'to be' thus and 'not to be', that is, affirms thus and removes thus: so that it both affirms and removes present time, as "Socrates is", "Socrates is not"; and affirms and removes the past, as "Socrates was", "Socrates was not"; and in the same way the future, "Socrates will be", "Socrates will not be". Therefore in all these times the whole force of the statement lies in something's being or not being, that is, in affirming and removing;

passages.original: dicit illa oppositione affirmationem et negationem integram constituere contradictionem, quae idem subjectum habeant, idem etiam prædicatum, ut neque subjectum neque praedicatum plura significet,alioqui non erit contradictio nec aliqua oppositio ut cum dieo, Socrates albus est, et alius dicit, Æthiops albus non est, haec affirmatio atque negatio non sunt oppositæ, idcirco quia est aliud subjectum et idem prædicatum.In affirmatione enim Socrates subjectus fuit,in negatione Ælhiops. Rursus cum dico,Socrates albus est, et alius dicit, Socrates philosophus non est, nee haec rursus negatio contra affirmationem retinet oppositionem, ideo quia aliud praedicatum in utrisque proponitur, in affirmatione enim album prædicatur ad Socratem, in negatione philosopbus.Quod si utraque suntdi- versa,multo magis nulla fit oppositio, ut cum dico Socrates philosophus est,si respondeat alius, Plato Romanus non est, hic neque idem subjectum est, neque idem prædicatum,et plus istæ diversæ sunt,et nulla contra se oppositione compositæ, atque ideo possunt utraeque simul esse veræ, etsi ita contingit utræque simul esse falsæ, nec non etiam una vera,altera falsa.Quæ enim se non perimunt, nihil eas impedit aut utrasque falsas,aut utrasque veras, aut unam veram,falsum alterareperiri : quare quorum vel aliud subjectum est, vel aliud prædicatum, illa opposita esse non dicimus ;
passages.english: He says that an affirmation and a negation make up a complete contradiction by that opposition when they have the same subject and also the same predicate, in such a way that neither the subject nor the predicate signifies several things; otherwise there will be no contradiction, nor any opposition. For example, when I say, "Socrates is white," and someone else says, "The Ethiopian is not white," this affirmation and negation are not opposed, because the subject is different and the predicate the same. For in the affirmation Socrates was the subject, in the negation the Ethiopian. Again, when I say, "Socrates is white," and someone else says, "Socrates is not a philosopher," this negation in turn does not hold an opposition against the affirmation either, because a different predicate is put forward in each: in the affirmation "white" is predicated of Socrates, in the negation "philosopher." But if both are different, much more is there no opposition, as when I say, "Socrates is a philosopher," and someone else replies, "Plato is not a Roman": here there is neither the same subject nor the same predicate, and these are all the more different and composed with no opposition to one another, and so both can be true at the same time, even if it so happens that both are false at the same time, and also that one is true and the other false. For nothing prevents statements that do not destroy one another from being found either both false, or both true, or one true and the other false. Therefore we say that those which have either a different subject or a different predicate are not opposed;

passages.original: unde fit ut nec illa quoque quaeplurasignificant, si subjecta aut praedicata sint contradictoriam negationem valeant cu- stodire.Si quis enim nomen aequivocum subjiciat, et aliud prædicet, ut si quis contra hujusmodi affirmationem constituat negationem, nou faciet oppo. sitionem : ut cum dico, Cato se Uticæ occidit, nomen hoc quod dicitur Cato æquivocum est. Potest enim et Orator intelligi, et hic qui exercitum duxit in Africam.Si quis igitur dicat, Cato se Uticæ occidit, potest fortasse intelligi de Catone Marciae. Si quis respondeat,Cato se Utica; non occidit,potest de Catone Censorio constituisse negationem. Sed quoniam diversus estCato Censorius a Catone Marciae, et nomen ipsum Catonis dlversa significat, diversæ a se affirmatio et negatio.Et id non omnino perimit negatio, quod constituit affirmatio.
passages.english: Hence it comes about that those [terms] which signify many things, if they are subjects or predicates, cannot preserve a contradictory negation either. For if someone makes an equivocal name the subject and predicates something else, as if someone sets up a negation against such an affirmation, he will not produce an opposition: as when I say 'Cato killed himself at Utica', this name 'Cato' is equivocal. For it can be understood both as the Orator and as the one who led an army into Africa. If then someone says 'Cato killed himself at Utica', it may perhaps be understood of Marcia's Cato. If someone replies 'Cato did not kill himself at Utica', he may have framed the negation about Cato the Censor. But since Cato the Censor is different from Marcia's Cato, and the name 'Cato' itself signifies different things, the affirmation and negation are different from each other. And the negation does not at all destroy what the affirmation asserted.
passages.notes: Boethius' identifications of the Catos (Orator/Censor vs. the one who led an army to Africa, Marcia's husband, i.e. Cato of Utica) are as in the text.

passages.original: Quæ omnia in sophisticis elenchis diligentissime prosecutus est.Nunc pauca commemorans distulit in illis libris integram disputationem.Est autem enuntiatio de eo quod est aliquid esse, vel non esse ; affirmatio quidem de eo quod est esse,ut Plato philosophus est; negatio vero de eo quod est non esse, ut Plato philosophus non est. Hæc utraque enuntiatio Plata philosophus est, Plato philosophus non est, sese perimentia et in contrarium quasi quodam locata litigio faciunt contradictionem.
passages.english: All of which he pursued most carefully in the Sophistical Refutations. Now, mentioning a few things, he has deferred the full discussion to those books. A statement, then, is about that which is, [saying] that something is or is not: an affirmation about that which is, that it is, as 'Plato is a philosopher'; a negation about that which is, that it is not, as 'Plato is not a philosopher'. These two statements, 'Plato is a philosopher' and 'Plato is not a philosopher', destroying each other and set in opposition as if in a kind of quarrel, make a contradiction.

passages.original: Contradictio vero est oppositio affirmationis et negationis,in uaneque ambas falsas,ne- que ambas veras esse contingit,sed unam semper veram,aIteram vero falsam Si qua autem sunt hujusmodi,in quibus verum falsumque affirmatio negatioque non dividat, in illis aliquid diversum, et non ad oppositionem integrum reperitur. Dicit autem Porphyrius argumentum esse ad id quod dicimus affirmationem negationi ita oportere opponi, ut una vera opposita in alteram mox falsitas veniat, communem inter nos consuetudinem colloquendi. Quando enim quis aliquid esse dixerit et idem alius negaverit, unum ipsorum verum dicere, mentiri alium suspicamur.AmpliuB quoque.
passages.english: A contradiction is the opposition of an affirmation and a negation, in which it cannot happen that both are false or both true, but one is always true and the other false. If there are any of such a kind that the affirmation and negation do not divide true and false between them, in them something different is found, and not something complete for opposition. Porphyry says that the argument for what we say — that an affirmation must be opposed to a negation in such a way that when one is true, falsity at once comes into the other, its opposite — is our common habit of conversing. For when someone has said that something is and another has denied the same, we suppose that one of them speaks the truth and the other lies. Further also.
passages.notes: 'Amplius quoque' ends abruptly; the sentence continues in the following text.

passages.original: Videmus namque alias esse in rebus hujusmodi qualitates,quæ in aliam convenire non possunt, nisi in unam quamcumque particularem singularemque substantiam: alia est enim qualitas singularis, ut Platonis vel Socratis; alia est quae communicata cum pluribus totam se singulis et omnibus præbet,ut est ipsa humanitas. Est enim quaedam hujusmodi qualitas,quæ et in singulis tota sit, et in omnibus tota.
passages.english: For we see that there are in things some qualities of such a kind that they cannot fit into another, except into one particular and singular substance, whichever it is: for one quality is singular, like that of Plato or Socrates; another is that which, shared with many, offers itself whole to each and to all, as is humanity itself. For there is a quality of this kind which is whole in each individual and whole in all.

passages.original: Ergo quoniam necesse est, aut aliquid alicui inesse dicere, aut aliquid alicui non inesse, illud quoque necesse est ut intelligamus cui inesse aliquid dicimus,aut universale esse, ut cum dicimushomo albus est, albedinem uniyersali rei inesse monstramus,id esthomini,autcerteparticulare ac singulare, ut si quis dicat,Socrates albus est,a]bedinem enim Socrati singularisubstantiæ et proprietati incommu- nicabili inesse significavit;sed in singularibus sive affirmetur aliquid, sive negetur, unus oppositionis modus est, quod vim contradictionis obtineat.
passages.english: Therefore, since it is necessary either to say that something belongs to something or that something does not belong to something, it is also necessary for us to understand that what we say something belongs to is either universal—as when we say "man is white," we show that whiteness belongs to a universal thing, that is, to man—or else particular and singular, as if someone should say, "Socrates is white," for he has signified that whiteness belongs to Socrates, a singular substance and an incommunicable property. But in singulars, whether something is affirmed or denied, there is one mode of opposition that holds the force of contradiction.

passages.original: Quocirca possunt indefinitae aliquando significare contraria,quoniam eo ipso quod sunt indefinitae nihil eas prohibet ad contrariorum significationem universa. Hum que reduci.Ethæc quidem sententia habet aliquid rationis, non tamen integre id quod ab Aristotele dicitur ostendit, et meliorem sententiam sponte reje- cit, quam Porphyrius approbavit. Sunt enim quædam negationes quæ intra se affirmationis ejus quam negant retineant contrarietatem, ut in eo quod est, sanus est, et non est sanus, id quod dicitur non est sanus significat aeger est, quod est contrarium sano esse.
passages.english: Therefore indefinite [propositions] can sometimes signify contraries, since by the very fact that they are indefinite nothing prevents them from being brought to the signification of universal contraries. And this view indeed has some reason, yet it does not fully show what Aristotle says, and it has deliberately rejected the better view, which Porphyry approved. For there are some negations which retain within themselves the contrariety of the affirmation they deny, as in 'is healthy' and 'is not healthy': what is said, 'is not healthy', signifies 'is sick', which is contrary to being healthy.
passages.notes: 'universa. Hum que' read as 'universalium'.

passages.original: sunt, ut contra universalem affimationem illa opponatur quæ sub universali negatione est, contra universalem negationem illa contradictorie constituatur quæ est sub universali affirmatione, quod scilicet volens Aristoteles ostendero sic ait:
passages.english: [...] are, so that against the universal affirmation there is opposed the one that lies under the universal negation, [and] against the universal negation there is set contradictorily the one that lies under the universal affirmation; which Aristotle, wishing to show, speaks thus:
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; the opening 'sunt' completes a clause from the preceding text. The contradictories meant are the particular negative and the particular affirmative that sit diagonally beneath the universals.

passages.original: in enuntiatione propositio, vel de alio subjecto prædicet idem quod affirmatio ante posuerat,non erunt ilia affirmatio negatioque oppositæ,sed tantum a se diversæ; neque enim se perimunt. Et hanc rem de- monstrativam addidit, et quae esset argumentum unius affirmationis præter unam negationem esse non posse, sive in singularibus, ut in eo quod ipse dicit exemplo, est Socrates albus, non est Socrates albus ; sive in universalibus universaliter prædicatis,cum his particulares in oppositione contradictoe riae constituuntur, ut in universali universaliter affirmativa,omnis homo albus est,in universali particulariter negativa prædicetur,non omnis homo albus ;
passages.english: in the statement, the proposition, or if it predicates of another subject the same thing that the affirmation had posited before, that affirmation and negation will not be opposed, but only different from each other; for they do not destroy each other. And he added this demonstrative point, which would be a proof that there cannot be more than one negation for one affirmation, whether in singulars, as in the example he himself gives, "Socrates is white," "Socrates is not white"; or in universals predicated universally, when particulars are set against them in contradictory opposition, as when against the universal affirmative taken universally, "every man is white," there is predicated the universal negative taken particularly, "not every man is white";
passages.notes: The opening is a sentence fragment continuing from the preceding context; "propositio" here seems to stand for the negation.

passages.original: Cur autem hoc dixerit, sequens monstret oratio.Si enim ita facienda propositio est, ut con Ira affirmationem hujusmodi opponatur negatio, quæ in oppositione verum falsumque dividit, ut una vera,altera falsa sit, unam oportet esse affirmatione et unam negationem, quod cOnlingit, si neque subjectum neque prædicatum multa significet. Quod si plura designet et sit æquivocum, non erit in hujusmodi propositionis una semper vera,altera falsa.Herminus vero sic sentit, Quod ait Aristoteles : Sin vero duobus nomen unum est positum, ex quibus non est unum, non est una affirmatio nec una negatio,ut in eo,inquit, quod est, homo gressibilis est, quoniam quod dicimus gressibile,potest et bipes esse, et quadrupes, et multipes animal demonstrari.
passages.english: Why he said this, the following discussion may show. For if a proposition is to be formed so that against such an affirmation a negation is opposed which in the opposition divides true and false, so that one is true and the other false, there must be one affirmation and one negation, which happens if neither the subject nor the predicate signifies many things. But if it designates several things and is equivocal, in such a proposition one will not always be true and the other false. Herminus, however, takes it thus, that what Aristotle says — 'But if one name is assigned to two things from which no one thing is made, there is not one affirmation nor one negation' — [applies], he says, as in 'a man is footed', since what we call 'footed' can be shown to be an animal that is two-footed, four-footed and many-footed.

passages.original: Cras non omnes Athenienses bello navali pugnaturi sunt. In singularibus autem talis est: Cras Socrates in pala:- stra pu"naturus est. Cras Socrates in palaestra pu- gnaturus non est. Non autem oportet ignorare non essesimiliter contingentes has quæ dicunt Socrates morietur, et Socrates non morietur,et illas quae di- cunt,Socrates morietur cras,Socrates non morietur cras.Illæ enim superiores omnino contingentes non sunt, sed nun necessariæ. Morietur enim Socrates ex necessitate, hae vero quae tempus diffiniunt, nec ipsae in numero contingentium recipiuntur,idcirco quod nobis quidem cras moriturum esse :.ocratem incertum est.Naturæ autem incertum non est.Atque ideo necDeo quoque incertum est, qui ipsam naturam optime novit.Sed illae sunt propriae contingentes,quæ neque in natura sunt,neque in necessitate, sed aut in casu, aut in libero arbitrio,ad in possibilitate naturæ.Ex casu quidem ut cum egredior domo amicum videam,non ob hoc egrediens.Ex libero ar- bitrio,ut quod possum et velle et non velle an velim hoc antequam fiat incertum est.
passages.english: "Tomorrow not all Athenians are going to fight in a naval battle." In singulars, however, it is of this kind: "Tomorrow Socrates is going to fight in the palaestra," "Tomorrow Socrates is not going to fight in the palaestra." But one should not be unaware that those which say "Socrates will die" and "Socrates will not die" are not contingent in the same way as those which say "Socrates will die tomorrow," "Socrates will not die tomorrow." For the former are not contingent at all, but necessary: for Socrates will die of necessity. But these which define a time are not themselves counted among contingents either, because it is uncertain to us, indeed, that Socrates will die tomorrow, but it is not uncertain to nature; and therefore it is not uncertain to God either, who knows nature itself best of all. But those are properly contingent which are neither in nature nor in necessity, but either in chance, or in free will, or in the possibility of nature. From chance, as when I go out of the house and see a friend, though not going out for this reason. From free will, as when I am able both to will and not to will: whether I will this is uncertain before it happens.
passages.notes: "ad in possibilitate" read as "aut in possibilitate."

passages.original: Est enim utrumlibet quod,vel ad esse,vel ad non esse aequaliter se habet, id est neque illud esse necesse sit,neque non esse necesse sit.Putaveruntau- tem quidam,quorum stoici quoque sunt,Aristotelem dicere,in futuro contingentes nec veras,nec falsas, quod enim dixit nihil se magis ad esse habere quam ad non esse,hoc putaverunt tanquam nihil eas interesset falsas an veras putari, neque veras enim neque falsas esse arbitrati sunt, sed falsum eat; non enim Aristoteles hoc dicit, quod utraeque nee veræ, nec falsas sint,sed quod una quidem ipsarum quælibet aut vera aut falsaest.Non tamen quemadmodum in præteritis definite,nec quemadmodum in præsentibus,sed enuntiativarum vocum duplicem,quodammodo esse naturam,quarum quaedam easentinqui- bus non modo verum et falsum invenirelur,sed in quibus,etiam unam esse definite veram,alteram definite falsam, in aliis vero una quidem vera, altera falsa, sed indefinite, et commutabiliter, et hoc per suam naturam,non ad nostram ignorantiam atque notitiam.
passages.english: For that is 'either way' (utrumlibet) which stands equally toward being or toward not being, that is, it is neither necessary that it be nor necessary that it not be. But some people, among whom are also the Stoics, thought that Aristotle says that contingent [propositions] about the future are neither true nor false. For what he said, that [a proposition] is no more disposed toward being than toward not being, they took to mean that it made no difference whether they were thought false or true; for they judged that they were neither true nor false. But this is false. For Aristotle does not say this, that both are neither true nor false, but that any one of them is indeed either true or false, yet not definitely, as in past [events], nor as in present ones. Rather, [he says] that the nature of enunciative utterances is in a certain way twofold: some of them are such that in them not only are truth and falsity found, but in which also one is definitely true and the other definitely false; in others, however, one is indeed true and the other false, but indefinitely and changeably, and this by their own nature, not in relation to our ignorance and knowledge.
passages.notes: 'eat' read as 'est'; 'easent' as 'essent'.

passages.original: Qui autem ita dicit,cras erit bellum navale,quasi necesse sit, ita pronuntiat,quod si evenerit,non jam idcirco quia prædixit,verum dixerit,quoniam id quod eon- tingenter eventurum erat, necessarie futurum esse prædixit.Non ergo in eventu est falsitas,sed in pra?- dicationis modo.Quemadmod um enim si quisSocrate ambulante dicat: Socrates ex necessitate ambulat, ille mentitus est non in eo quod Socrates ambulat, sed in eo quod ille ex necessitate eum ambulare prae- dicayh, ita quoque in hoc : Qui dicit quoniam erit aliquid, etiam si hoc fiat, ille tamen falsus est,non in eo quod factum est,sed in eo quod non ita factum est, ut ille prædixit futurum.
passages.english: But someone who says "tomorrow there will be a naval battle" as though it were necessary pronounces it in such a way that, if it happens, he will not on that account have spoken truly because he predicted it, since what was going to happen contingently he predicted would come about necessarily. So the falsity is not in the outcome but in the mode of prediction. For just as, if while Socrates is walking someone should say, "Socrates walks of necessity," he has spoken falsely not in that Socrates walks, but in that he predicated that he walks of necessity, so too in this case: whoever says that something will be, even if it happens, is nevertheless false, not in that it happened, but in that it did not happen in the way he predicted it would.

passages.original: Et ex bac autem quæ estutrumlibet possibilitate etiam ilia liberi arbi. trii ratio venit. Si enim non esset fieri aliquid possibile, sed omnia aut ex necessitate esent, aut ex necessitate non essent, liberum arbitrium non maneret. Recte igitur nec omnia casu, ut Epicurus, nec necessitate omnia, ut Stoicus, nec rursus omnia libero arbitrio fieri proposuit. Sed cuncta permi- scens, in permisto mundo permistas quoque rerum causas esse proposuit, utaliæ quidem ex necessitate, alix vero casu, vel libero arbitrio,vel postremo possi.
passages.english: And from this possibility which is 'either way' there also comes that account of free will. For if it were not possible for something to come about, but all things either were of necessity or of necessity were not, free will would not remain. Rightly, therefore, he laid down neither that all things happen by chance, as Epicurus [held], nor all by necessity, as the Stoic [held], nor again all by free will. But mixing all together, he laid down that in a mixed world the causes of things too are mixed, so that some happen of necessity, others by chance, or by free will, or finally by possibility.
passages.notes: The final word 'possi-bilitate' runs into the following context.

passages.original: Sin vero marmoreum Socratem dicamus,quoniam marmoreum Socratem sedere necesse est, si fortasse se- dens formatus sit, verum est, et simpliciter de tali Socrate necessitas poterit prædicari. De ipso autem Socratesimplicitertalis necessitas non dicitur.Nequo enim fieri potest ut Socrates ex necessitate sedeat nisi fortasse cum sedet, tunc emim cum sedet, quoniam sedet et non potest non sedere, ex necessitate sedet alioqui simpliciter et non ex necessitate sedet, sed contingenter.
passages.english: But if we speak of a marble Socrates, since a marble Socrates must sit if he happens to have been sculpted sitting, it is true, and necessity can be predicated simply of such a Socrates. But of Socrates himself such necessity is not stated simply. For it cannot be that Socrates sits of necessity except perhaps when he is sitting; for then, when he sits, since he sits and cannot not sit, he sits of necessity; otherwise he sits simply and not of necessity, but contingently.

passages.original: Sin vero esset res quæ varietate naturae nunquam perpetuo permaneret,in orationibus quoque fixa veritas non esset, et nulla per hujusmodi orationes demonstratio proveniret. Hoc ergo sumens Aristoteles ut optime dictum, sic ait : Quare qnoniam orationes similiter veræ sunt,quemadmodum et res, manifeslum est quoniam quæcun-que sic se habent,ut utrumlibet sint, et contraria ipsorum contingere possint, necesse est similiter se habere et contradictionem.
passages.english: But if there were a thing which, owing to the variability of [its] nature, never remained permanently, there would also be no fixed truth in statements, and no demonstration would arise through statements of this kind. Taking this, then, as excellently said, Aristotle speaks thus: 'Hence, since statements are true in the same way as things are, it is clear that whatever things are so disposed that they are either way, and their contraries can happen, the contradiction too must be similarly disposed.'

passages.original: Ex infinito quidem quemadmodum cum dico, non homo ambulat, ex finito au- tem et simplici, ut homo ambulat. Hujus autem quae ex finito et simplici est, species sunt duae, quas aut universale nomen subjicit, ut homo ambulat, aut singulare, ut Socrates ambulat. Quare ita fit divisio. Omnium enuntiationum simplicium,quaeduobusterminis constant,aliæ sunt ex infinito nomine subjecto, aliae vero ex finito et simplici. Earum quae simplex habent subjectum,alife sunt quae universale simplex subjiciunt, aliae quae singulare.
passages.english: From an indefinite [name], as when I say, "not-man walks"; from a definite and simple one, as "man walks." Of the one from a definite and simple [name] there are two species: those in which a universal name is the subject, as "man walks," or a singular one, as "Socrates walks." So the division runs thus: of all simple statements consisting of two terms, some are from an indefinite name as subject, others from a definite and simple one. Of those that have a simple subject, some take a universal simple [name] as subject, others a singular one.
passages.notes: "infinitum nomen" rendered "indefinite name" (Aristotle's onoma aoriston, e.g. "not-man").

passages.original: Non enim positumesttertium prasdicatursolum.Sed adjacens tertium secundo Joco, et (quemadmodum dictum est) accidenter praedicatur. Potest autem et sic intelligi, idcirco dixisse Aristotelem est in his tertium adjacens praedicari,quoniampossit aliquoties et per se praedicari, ut si quis dicat Socrates philosophusest,ut propositiohaechocsentiat:Soorates philosophus vivit.Estenim pro vivit positum est. Si quis ergo sicdicat,duo inveniuntursubjecta.Est vero solum praedicatur, non etiam adjacens.
passages.english: For "third" was not set down as predicated alone, but as adjacent third in the second place, and (as has been said) it is predicated accidentally. It can also be understood this way: Aristotle said "is" is predicated in these as a third adjacent because it can sometimes also be predicated by itself, as if someone says "Socrates is a philosopher" so that this proposition means "Socrates the philosopher lives." For "is" has been put for "lives." If someone speaks thus, two subjects are found, and "is" alone is predicated, not as adjacent.

passages.original: Nam sicut in his quae infinitas sunt et indeterminatae duæ sunt oppositiones,una simplicis negationis et simplicisaffirmationis,alterainfinilae affirmationis et infinitae negationis.Quatuor autem propositiones,quod supra'jam dictumest,itaquoque in iis quae determinationem secundum universalitatem particularitatemque habent,quatuor fiunt propositiones et oppositio duplex.Oppositio enim una est universalis affirmationis simplicis,et particularis negationis simplicis,ut est,omnis homo justus est, non omnis homo justus est, et haecest quidem una oppositio.Alia vero infinitae universalis affirmationis,et infinitæ parlicularis negationis, ut est, omnis homo non justus est, non omnis homo non justus est. Quare hic quoque cum duae sint oppositiones, erunt sine dubio propositiones quatuor,sicut in his de quibus supra dixerat,quae sci licet,determinatione carebant.Alii vero qui Aristotelis animum penitus inspexerint,non aiunt similiter solum se habere determinatas propositiones,ad numerum oppositionum et propositionum,sed etiam ad consequentiam,nam quae est consequentia negationum ad affirmationes in his propositionibus simplicibus et infinitis,quæ praeter determinationum dicuntur,eadem similitudo habetur,el in iis quae cum determinatione proferuntur.Sed quoniam non in omnibus omnia similia habent,idcirco addidit notans,sed non similiter angu- Jares contingit esse veras,contingit autem aliquando.
passages.english: For just as in those that are infinite and indeterminate there are two oppositions, one of the simple negation and simple affirmation, the other of the infinite affirmation and infinite negation, but four propositions, as was already said above, so too in those which have a determination according to universality and particularity there come to be four propositions and a twofold opposition. For one opposition is of the simple universal affirmation and the simple particular negation, as 'every man is just', 'not every man is just'; and this is one opposition. The other is of the infinite universal affirmation and the infinite particular negation, as 'every man is not-just', 'not every man is not-just'. Hence here too, since there are two oppositions, there will without doubt be four propositions, just as in those of which he had spoken above, namely those that lacked determination. Others, however, who have looked more deeply into Aristotle's mind, say that the determinate propositions are alike not only with respect to the number of oppositions and propositions, but also with respect to their implication: for whatever implication of negations to affirmations there is in those simple and infinite propositions which are stated without determinations, the same likeness is found also in those which are uttered with a determination. But since they do not have everything alike in all respects, he therefore added, noting it: 'but it does not happen in the same way that the diagonal ones are true; yet it does happen sometimes.'
passages.notes: 'angulares' = diagonally opposed propositions in the square of opposition. 'praeter determinationum' read as 'praeter determinationem'.

passages.original: Manifestum est autem, quoniam etiam in singularibus, si est verum interrogatum negare quod et affirmareverum est, ut, Putasne Socrates sapiens est? Non. Socrates igitur non sapiens est. In universalibus uero non est vera quæ similiter dicitur; vera est autem negatio, ut,Pulasne omnis homo sapiens est Non. Omnis igitur homo non sapiens est: hoc enim est falsum, sed, non igitur omnis homo sapiens est, vera est ;
passages.english: It is clear, too, that in singulars, if it is true to deny what is asked, it is also true to affirm [the negative], as: "Do you think Socrates is wise?" "No." "Therefore Socrates is not-wise." But in universals the one stated in a similar way is not true; the negation is true, as: "Do you think every man is wise?" "No." "Therefore every man is not-wise": for this is false; but "therefore not every man is wise" is true;
passages.notes: Latin cannot distinguish "is not wise" from "is not-wise"; the argument (from Aristotle's text) requires the indefinite predicate "not-wise" in the inferred statements.

passages.original: atque ille respondeat: Non, nos vere concludere possumus : Socrates igilur nun Romanus est.Facientes ex negalione quam ille respondebat, et ex nomine quod in proposiliore praedicavimus affirmationem ex infinito nominenuae dicit: Socrates non sapiens est, vel Socrates non Romanus est. Has enim atfirmaliones esse ex infinito nomine supra monstratum est. Si igilur eodem modo aliquis in universalibus subjectis interroget dicens ;
passages.english: and he answers: No, we can truly conclude: Therefore Socrates is not Roman, making an affirmation from the negation he gave in answer and from the name we predicated in the proposition, [an affirmation] from an indefinite name, which says: Socrates is not-wise, or Socrates is not-Roman. For it was shown above that these are affirmations from an indefinite name. If, then, someone in the same way asks about universal subjects, saying:
passages.notes: The scanned text is corrupt in places ("proposiliore", "nominenuae"); read as propositione and nomine quae.

passages.original: Cum igitur ita sint affirmationes positae et negalionesquae simplex quidem subjectum habent, infinitum vero vel simplex prædicatum, nunc Aristoteles dicit quoniam hre propositiones qnae subje.ctum babentinfinitum nulliillarumsuperiorumqu es disposuimus idem significant: haec enim quae dicil, esl omnis non homo justus, non consenlil ei quap dicil ,eslomois homo justus,nec rursus ei quae dicit,est omnis horno non justus, nec his rursus quae sunl, nullus est homo justus, vel nullus est homo non jusies ;
passages.english: Since, then, the affirmations and negations which have a simple subject and an infinite or simple predicate have been laid out thus, Aristotle now says that these propositions which have an infinite subject signify the same as none of those earlier ones which we arranged: for this one which says 'every not-man is just' does not agree with the one which says 'every man is just', nor again with the one which says 'every man is not-just', nor again with these, 'no man is just' or 'no man is not-just';

passages.original: Multum enim inleresl in eo quod ait Cicpro, Ad hanc Ie amenliam natura peperit, voluntas exercuit fortuna servavit, ita dixisse ut dictum est, an ita, Ad hanc te amentiam peperit natura, exercuit voluntas,servavit fortuna. Sic enim minor est sententiae magnitudo, minusque in ea lucet id quod si sic componatur eminet, et sese vel nolentibus hominum auribus animisque patefacit. Rursus cum dicit Virgilius : Pacique imponere morem, potuisset servare metrum, si ita dixisset, moremque imponere paci, sed esset debilior sonus, nec in eo ictu versus tam praeclare ut nunc compositus diccreretur. Ergo non idem valet oratoribus vel poetis verborum nominumque ordo mutamus.
passages.english: For there is a great difference, in what Cicero says, 'To this madness nature bore you, will trained you, fortune preserved you,' whether it is said as it was said, or thus: 'To this madness bore you nature, trained you will, preserved you fortune.' For thus the grandeur of the sentence is smaller, and what stands out when it is arranged in the first way shines less in it, [that which] reveals itself even to the unwilling ears and minds of men. Again, when Virgil says 'and to impose a custom on peace' (pacique imponere morem), he could have kept the metre if he had said 'and a custom to impose on peace' (moremque imponere paci), but the sound would be weaker, and the line would not be perceived in that stroke as splendidly as it now is composed. Therefore the order of verbs and nouns, [if] we change it, does not have the same force for orators or poets.
passages.notes: Final clause 'ordo mutamus' is ungrammatical; perhaps 'ordo si mutamus' or 'ordo mutatus'.

passages.original: Quisquis dialectica utitur interrogatione, hic aut simpliciter interrogat, atque unam propositionem in interrogatione ponit, ut contra eam sit una responsio, aut utrasque interrogans dicit, ad quas non fit simplex responsio, sed una tota propositio respondetur. Si quis enim dicat interrogans : Socrates animal est? Contra hanc talis est responsio, aut ita, aut non. Si quis vero hoc modo iuterroget: Socrates animal est, an non ? Contra hanc non est una responsio. Si enim respondetur ita, de qua annueris ignoratur, de affirmatione an de negatione ;
passages.english: Whoever uses dialectical questioning either asks simply and puts one proposition in the question, so that there is one answer to it, or asks both [parts], to which there is not a simple answer, but a whole proposition is given in reply. For if someone asks, "Is Socrates an animal?" the answer to this is either "yes" or "no." But if someone asks in this way: "Is Socrates an animal or not?" there is not one answer to this. For if "yes" is answered, it is unknown which you assented to, the affirmation or the negation;

passages.original: Suni autem alia quae, si per se et disjuncta praedicentur, vera sunt; sin vero CODjuncta dicantur, veritatem in prædicatione non re tenent; quæ ergo sit horum differentia, oportet agnosci. Si quis enim dicai, Socrates animal est, verum dixerit ; si quis rursus praedicet, quoniam Socrates bipes est, hoc quoque verum est ; quae si conjuncta dicantur,ut est,Socrales animal bipes est, a propria veritate non discrepat, atque haec quidem in genere et differentia, ea quae substantialis est Socrati.Quodsi deaccidente quoquedicalur, potestidem nihil ominusevenire.
passages.english: But there are other things which, if they are predicated by themselves and separately, are true; but if they are said conjoined, they do not retain truth in the predication. What, then, the difference between these is must be recognized. For if someone says, "Socrates is an animal," he will have spoken truly; if someone again predicates that Socrates is two-footed, this too is true; and if these are said conjoined, as in "Socrates is a two-footed animal," it does not depart from its proper truth, and this indeed in the case of genus and differentia, which is substantial to Socrates. But if it is said of an accident too, the same can nonetheless happen.
passages.notes: The passage sits awkwardly with its context: the opening sentence speaks of predicates true separately but not true conjoined, yet the examples (and the context before and after) illustrate predicates that remain true when conjoined. The order of sentences in the edition may be disturbed. Scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'Suni' for 'Sunt', 'CODjuncta' for 'conjuncta', 'non re tenent' for 'non retinent', 'dicai' for 'dicat').

passages.original: Quae superius comprehendit, ea nunc apertissima ratione determinat dicens, de his solis extra praedicalis veraciter non posse unam prædicationem fieri veram, si conjuncta sint, quæcunque aut accidentia sunt eidem, aut cum unum alii accidit, accidens aliud de illo accidenti praedicatur. Si quis enim de Socrate dicat. quoniam Socrates citharcedus est, rursus Socrates bonus est, si utraque vere praedicet, duo accidentia de uno subjecto praedicavil, id est de Socrate. Quocirca non potest ex his fieri una praedicatio, ut dicatur, Socrates citharoedus bona est ;
passages.english: What he set out above, he now defines by the clearest reasoning, saying that of these alone, among the things truly predicated outside [each other], one true predication cannot be made if they are conjoined: whatever are either accidents of the same thing, or, when one accident belongs to another, another accident is predicated of that accident. For if someone says of Socrates that Socrates is a cithara-player, and again that Socrates is good, if he predicates both truly, he has predicated two accidents of one subject, that is, of Socrates. Therefore one predication cannot be made from these, so that it is said, "Socrates is a good cithara-player";
passages.notes: 'extra praedicatis veraciter' is obscure; perhaps 'of things truly predicated separately'. 'bona' read as 'bonus'.

passages.original: Vel etiam, quando inest, semper non verum est, quando uero non inest, non semper verum est, ut Homerus est aliquid, ut poeta, ergo etiam est, an non. Secundum accidens enim prædicatur esse de Homero, quoniam est porta, sed non secundum se prædicatur de Homero, quoniam est.
passages.english: Or also, when it inheres, it is always not true, but when it does not inhere, it is not always true: as 'Homer is something, as a poet; therefore he also is'—or not? For 'is' is predicated of Homer accidentally, because he is a poet, but it is not predicated of Homer in itself, that he is.
passages.notes: The first sentence is obscure and possibly corrupt. 'porta' read as 'poeta'.

passages.original: Quoniam enim quod non est opinabile est, idcirco secundo loco de eo quod non esi, verbum est praedicamus. Quare non possumus simpliciter dicere esse quod non est. Idcirco enim opinabile est, quia non est. Scibile enirn esset, si per se esset, non opinabile, sicut Homerus idcirco esse dicilur, quia poeta est, non quia per se est. Vel cerie idcirco dicitur Homerus esse poeta, quia poesis ipsius exstat et perma- net, sicut aliquos in filiis saepe vivere dicimus.
passages.english: For since what is not is an object of opinion, therefore we predicate the verb 'is' of what is not in a secondary way. Hence we cannot say simply that what is not is. For it is an object of opinion precisely because it is not. For it would be an object of knowledge, not of opinion, if it were in itself; just as Homer is said to be because he is a poet, not because he is in himself. Or certainly Homer is said to be a poet because his poetry exists and endures, just as we often say that some people live on in their children.

passages.original: Omnis proposito aut sine ullo modo simpliciter pronuntiatur, ut Sperates ambulat, ut dies est, ve quidquidsimplicitur et sine ulla qualitate prsedicalur. Sunt autem aliae quae cum propriis dicuntur modis, ut est, Socrates velociler ambulat. Ambulationi enim Socratis modus est additus, cum dicimus eum velociter ambulare, quomodo enim ambulat, significat ad quod de ambulatione ejus velociter prædica mus. Similiter autem si quis dicat, Socrates bene doctus est, quemadmodum sit doctus ostendit, nec solum doctus dixil, sed modum quoque doctrinae Socratis adjunxil.
passages.english: Every proposition is either stated simply, without any mode, as "Socrates walks," or "it is day," or whatever is predicated simply and without any qualification. But there are others which are said with their own modes, as "Socrates walks quickly." For a mode has been added to Socrates' walking when we say that he walks quickly, since what we predicate of his walking, "quickly," signifies how he walks. Similarly, if someone says, "Socrates is well taught," he shows how he is taught, and he has not said only "taught," but has also added the mode of Socrates' learning.
passages.notes: 'ad quod' read as 'id quod'.

passages.original: ut in eo quod est contingens, si hoc perimere volumus, dicimus non contingens, et haec negatio est. Inconlingens autem nullus dixerit quod est privatio. Cum ergo contingens esse et possibile esse idem significent, multa in hin diversitas est secundum Porphyrium quae sunt necessaria et inesse tantum significantia, et contingentia vel possibilia. Quod enim esse aliquid dicitur, de praesenti temporejudicatur. Si quis enim nunc alicui est, hoc esse prædicatur.
passages.english: as in the case of 'contingent', if we want to do away with it, we say 'not contingent', and this is a negation; but no one would say 'uncontingent', which would be a privation. Although, then, 'to be contingent' and 'to be possible' signify the same thing, there is, according to Porphyry, great diversity among those which are necessary, those which signify merely inherence, and those which are contingent or possible. For what is said to be is judged with respect to present time: for if something now belongs to something, this is predicated as being.
passages.notes: 'Si quis enim nunc alicui est' read as 'si quid'.

passages.original: essentiam autempossibilitas,sed neque possibilitatem essentia vel necessitas, nec rursus necessitas essentiam sequebatur.Hic autem non esse,non possibile esse, et necesse non esse consequitur Sed neque non necesse esse, non esse sequitur, neque utrasque possibilitatis negatio, quæ non posse esse aliquid proponit.An magis illud dicendumest,quod sicut se in affirmationibus babet, ita quoque in negationibus, ut Theophrastus acutissime perspexit? Fuit enim consequentiainaffirmativis,ut necessitatem et esse consequeretur et possibilitas,possibilitatem vero nec esse sequeretur nec necessitas.Idem quoque penitus perspicientibus in negationibus apparebit, veniens namque negatio in necessario, faciensque hujusmodi negationem quæ dicit, non necesse est esse vim necessitatis infringit et totam propositionem ad possibile ducit,quodenim non necesse est esse, fracto rigore necessitatis ad possibilitatem perductum est,sed possibilitatem nec esse sequebatur nec necessitas Recte ergo fractam necessitatem et ad possibile perductam, cum negatio dicit non necesse esse, nec non esse,nec non contingere esse consequitur.
passages.english: but possibility did not follow [from] being, nor did being or necessity [follow from] possibility, nor again did necessity follow being. Here, however, 'not to be', 'not possible to be', and 'necessary not to be' follow; but 'not to be' does not follow 'not necessary to be', nor does the negation of either possibility, which states that something cannot be. Or should it rather be said that as it is in affirmations, so it is also in negations, as Theophrastus most acutely perceived? For the implication in affirmatives was such that possibility followed both necessity and being, while neither being nor necessity followed possibility. The same will also appear in negations to those who look closely: for a negation coming upon the necessary, and making a negation of this kind, which says 'it is not necessary to be', breaks the force of necessity and brings the whole proposition to the possible; for what is not necessary to be has, the rigidity of necessity being broken, been brought to possibility, but neither being nor necessity followed possibility. Rightly, then, when the negation says 'not necessary to be', [that is,] necessity broken and brought to the possible, neither 'not to be' nor 'not contingent to be' follows.
passages.notes: Opening clause begins mid-sentence; construction with following context. 'utrasque' read as 'utraque'.

passages.original: Eodem namque modo non dicitur possibile esse,quod vel ex falsitatein verum transitaliquando,vel rursus ex veritate in falsitate, ut si quis dicat nunc, quoniam dies esl,verum dixerit,idem si hoc nocte prædicet, falsum est, et hæc veritas propositionis in falsum estpermutata.Sicergo quædam sunt possibilitates, ut eas esse et non esse contingat, quæ non eodem modo dicuntur quemadmodum illæ qusemutabilemnaturam non habent,ut hae scilicet quas necessarias diximus, ut si quisdicatsolemmoveri,velsolem possibileesse moveri,hae nunquam ex veritate in falsitatem mutabuntur.Sed nunc de Aristotelis et Stoicorum dissensione tacendum est.Illud tamen solum studiosius per- quirendum est, quo loco sit ponenda negatio in his propositionibus, in quibus modus aliquis prædicatur, aut quae dicenturesse possibilesenuntiationes, contingentes et necessariae, et quacunque cum modo sint propositiones.IlIæ veraciter esse secundum modum sicut aliae secundum esse dicentur,in quarum significationibus rei de qua praedicantur subsistendi qualitas invenitur,ut cum dico.Socrates bene loquitur,modus quidam est bene loquendi Socratis.Ergo sicut in his propositionibus, quæcunque cujuslibet illius rei subsistentiam promittunt,ad ipsam subsistentiam negatio ponitur,ut cum dicimus,Socrates est,ad esse aptatur negatio,cum negamus, Socrates non est.
passages.english: For what sometimes passes from falsity into truth, or again from truth into falsity, is not called possible in the same way: for instance, if someone says now, while it is day, [that it is day], he will have spoken truly; if he predicates the same thing at night, it is false, and this truth of the proposition has been changed into falsity. So there are certain possibilities such that it happens that they are and are not, and these are not said in the same way as those which do not have a changeable nature, namely those which we called necessary; for instance, if someone says that the sun moves, or that it is possible for the sun to move, these will never be changed from truth into falsity. But for now we must be silent about the disagreement between Aristotle and the Stoics. Only this must be investigated more carefully: where the negation should be placed in those propositions in which some mode is predicated, or which are called possible, contingent and necessary statements, and whatever propositions are with a mode. Those will truly be said to be according to mode, as others according to being, in whose significations is found a quality of subsisting of the thing of which they are predicated, as when I say, "Socrates speaks well," there is a certain mode of Socrates' speaking well. So just as in those propositions which declare the subsistence of any thing whatever, the negation is placed with the subsistence itself, as when we say "Socrates is," the negation is fitted to "is" when we deny, "Socrates is not."
passages.notes: 'quoniam dies est' read as 'now that it is day'; the sentence is compressed. 'Illæ veraciter esse secundum modum...' is syntactically awkward; rendered by sense.

passages.original: Potest ergo quod est ambulobile, id est quod ambulare potest, non ambulare, et quod est visibile non videri.Quocirca docet non esse negationem ejus quæ dicit, posse esse eam quae proponit posse non esse.Idcirco quoniam utraeque sunt verae, ut in iis quæ(utipse ait)non semperactu sunt.Contingilenimunum ex utrisque quæ Aristoteles dicit, aut idem ipsum dicere et negare simuldeeodem,aut non secundum esse et non esse, quoe opponuntur, fieri affirmationes et negationes,id est ut aut idem sint affirmatio et negatio sibique consentiant,sisecundum esse et non esse in omnibus contradictio fit, ut est in eo quod est posse esse et posse non esse.
passages.english: Therefore what is walkable (ambulabile), that is, what is able to walk, can not walk, and what is visible [can] not be seen. For this reason he teaches that the [statement] which says 'it is possible not to be' is not the negation of the one which says 'it is possible to be'. [This is so] because both are true, as in those things which (as he himself says) are not always in actuality. For one of the two things which Aristotle mentions follows: either to affirm and deny the same thing at the same time about the same thing, or [to hold] that affirmations and negations do not come about according to 'to be' and 'not to be', which are opposed; that is, either the affirmation and the negation are the same and agree with each other, if contradiction arises in all cases according to 'to be' and 'not to be', as it does in 'it is possible to be' and 'it is possible not to be'.
passages.notes: Numerous scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'ambulobile' for ambulabile, 'Contingilenimunum' for Contingit enim unum, 'simuldeeodem' for simul de eodem). The sentence beginning 'Idcirco quoniam' is elliptical in the Latin.

passages.original: In his autem in quibus modus aliquis est,non dicitur aliquid esse,sed cum qualitate quadam esse,utesse quidem nee affirmatio ambigat,necnegatio.De qualitate autem, id est quomodo sit, tunc inter aliquos dubitatur, atque ideo ponente aliquo quoniam Socrates bene loquitur,non ponitur negatio,quoniam bene non loquitur,sed quoniam non bene loquitur. Idcirco quoniam(utdictum est) non ad esse vel ad ea verba quæ esse continent, et propositionem totam constituunt,sed potiusadmodum intendituranimus audientis,cum affirmatio aliquid esse prenuntiat.Si igitur hoc continet totius propositionis vim,quod autem propositionis vim continet prædicatur,etsecundum id quod praedicatur semperoppositiones fiunt, rectesolis modis visnegationisopponitur.His autem rationabiliter constitutis ilIud rursus exsequitur quod non modo contradictio non est posse esse et posse non esse, verum etiam hujusmodi proposttiones.quaecum modo sunt positæ,negationem tamen habent ad esse junctam,omninonegationesnon sunt,sed affirmationes, possunt enim earum negationes aliae reperiri.
passages.english: But in those in which there is some mode, it is not said that something is, but that it is with a certain quality, so that neither the affirmation nor the negation is in doubt about being. But about the quality, that is, how it is, there is then dispute among some, and therefore when someone posits that Socrates speaks well, the negation posited is not "[that] well he does not speak" but "[that] not-well he speaks." Therefore, since (as has been said) the mind of the hearer is directed not to "is" or to those verbs which contain "is" and make up the whole proposition, but rather to the mode, when the affirmation declares that something is [in a certain way]; if, then, this holds the force of the whole proposition, and what holds the force of the proposition is what is predicated, and oppositions are always made according to what is predicated, the force of the negation is rightly opposed to the modes alone. These things having been reasonably established, he goes on to show further that not only is "to be able to be" and "to be able not to be" not a contradiction, but also that propositions of this kind, which are posited with a mode but have the negation joined to "be," are not negations at all but affirmations, for other negations of them can be found.
passages.notes: The Latin distinction 'bene non loquitur' / 'non bene loquitur' is hard to reproduce in English; the point is that the negation attaches to the mode 'well'.

passages.original: alteram quae cum sit illud quoque habet,ut eam essenecesse sit.Nechocsolius Aristotelis subtilitas deprehendit, verum Diodorus quoque possibile ita diftinitdicens,qllod est aut non est-Unde Aristoteles id quod Diodorus ait non est, illud possibile putat, quod cum non fit fieri tamen polest. Quod autem dixit Diodorus, est id possibile, Aristoteles interpretatur, quod idcirco dicitur esse possibile, quia jam est actu.
passages.english: the other which, when it is, also has [this feature], that it is necessary for it to be. Nor did the subtlety of Aristotle alone detect this; Diodorus too defines the possible thus, saying [it is] what either is or is not. Hence what Diodorus calls 'is not', Aristotle considers to be that possible which, although it is not, can nevertheless come to be. And what Diodorus said, 'is', Aristotle interprets as that possible which is called possible because it already is in actuality.
passages.notes: 'diftinitdicens,qllod est aut non est' read as 'definit dicens, quod est aut non est'. Diodorus' definition seems compressed or corrupt here; the usual Diodoran definition is 'what either is or will be', so the text may be defective. 'cum non fit' taken as 'cum non sit'.

passages.original: De duabus igitur falsis quam mendaciorem ratioinvenit,eamdicimusvera3 opinioni magis esse contrariam.Sint igiturtresopiniones,una vera,duæ falsee : et sit quidem vera hæc quae id quod bonum est, bonum esse arbitratur, ea scilicet quam dicit Aristoteles opinionem esse boni quoniam bonum est, falsa vero una quae quod bonum est, bonum non esse dicit, ea est quam dicit Aristoteles falsa boni,quoniam non bonum.ReJiqua quae id quod bonum est, malum esse arbitratur,ea est quae ab Aristotele dicta est opinio boni quoniam malum est.
passages.english: Of the two false [opinions], then, the one which reason finds more false, we say is more contrary to the true opinion. Let there be, then, three opinions, one true and two false. Let the true one be this, which judges that what is good is good, namely the one which Aristotle calls the opinion of the good that it is good. One false [opinion] is that which says that what is good is not good; this is the one which Aristotle calls the false [opinion] of the good, that it is not good. The remaining one, which judges that what is good is bad, is the one which Aristotle has called the opinion of the good that it is bad.
passages.notes: 'mendaciorem' (literally 'more lying') rendered 'more false'. Scanning errors corrected ('vera3' for verae, 'ReJiqua' for Reliqua).
